In this course, we will work a lot with writing and applying functions; You’ve all been exposed to writing functions in previous courses - but just to make sure that everyone remembers the basic syntax in R, complete the following:

Write a function that computes energy produced from a photovoltaic system if you know the average annual solar radiation. You can use the following formula:
The energy produced by a solar panel system is given by
\[
E = A \cdot r \cdot H \cdot PR
\]
where:

\(E\) is the energy produced (kWh),
\(A\) is the solar panel area (m\(^2\)),
\(r\) is the panel yield (dimensionless, 0–1), representing manufacturer efficiency (typically \(\sim 0.2\)),
\(PR\) is the performance ratio (dimensionless, 0–1), accounting for site-specific losses (typically \(\sim 0.75\)),
\(H\) is the annual average solar radiation (kWh m\(^{-2}\)).

Write your function in R; make sure that you add documentation; include default values for r and PR in the function definition; save the function in a single file to upload to Canvas.

To summarize, submit the following by 8am Jan 8:

Fill out ‘get to know you’ survey on Canvas

A single R file that implements the solar energy yield function (on Canvas)

You don’t need to submit anything for the Lisa Felman Barrett blog - just think about the inverse inference problem in the context of the environment. We will discuss next class

title: Environmental Modelling
text:
Course description
Computer-based modeling and simulation are widely used tools in both practical environmental problem solving and in environmental research. Models give us a way to look at the world through a mixture of data and theory. A good model can help us to understand how the world works and how decisions that we make might change the world in ways that are important to us. There are many different types of models, from simple to complex, and models are often tailored to answer specific questions. This course will give you skills that help you to choose which model, or modeling technique, is right for you given the task at hand. The course will cover designing a new model and evaluating existing models. We will emphasize best practices, such as sensitivity and uncertainty analysis, that help to design and use models to reliably support environmental problem solving. This is a skills-based course and we will use R as our basic platform.
Class will include a mix of lectures and in-class hands-on examples, using students’ own computers. Discussion sections will elaborate on lecture topics and provide time to work on assignments with instructor and TA support.
The full syllabus (PDF) has grading, AI-tool policy and attendance details.

title: Environmental Modelling
text:
Protocols and guidance

Learning to program is hard and I may not always explain in a way that is accessible to you. If you don’t understand something, ask.

Ideally ask in class: you will help me learn how to explain (or find an answer if I don’t know it), and you will help others.
If you don’t feel comfortable asking in class, reach out to me or the TA.

Environmental modeling and the coding involved get better with practice and play. Don’t just read the Quarto documents: try the code, try variations on the ideas presented, make up stuff to try.
Programming means making mistakes. Expect it, stay calm and try again. If you get frustrated, step away and come back; be creative.
Respect and support each other.

When working in groups, pay attention to your partner. If they are not at your skill level, help them learn; we all have different backgrounds.
Listen. Different perspectives contribute to modeling. Ask questions and figure out how different people see the world (what is their conceptual model?).
You learn by helping others, so do that!

If you are really struggling, reach out to the TA or me. We can help (or if you just want to chat about something).

title: Types of Models
section: Conceptual Models: Things to think about
text:
Conceptual Models: Things to think about

What inputs/parameters will influence how a process/mechanism leads to the outputs you are interested in
Can you measure those inputs/parameters? If not is there a proxy? Or another model?
Are there features of the environment that influence the relationship between input/parameter and output?
Are there inputs/parameters that you want to vary across cenarios (things you’d want to ‘change’)
Time and Space (are you looking at a short or long terms behavior? do you care about spatial patterns? at what scale?)
What are some key assumptions?

title: Types of Models
text:
Stochastic - Deterministic
Stochastic: Model output is the probability of flood events of a magnitude greater than 500 m3/sec given rainfall probability distribution (artificial or generated from data) for a 100km2 watershed
Deterministic: Model output is the depth of flood given a rainfall event of 10cm over a 100km2 watershed
